Market regime: six questions, measured

28 Sep 2026 · closes to Fri 25 Sep 2026 · research, not buy rules · built 2026-09-28 13:42 UTC · the numbers live in regime.json · a proposal for a Hub panel: PROPOSAL.html
STATUS · all six studies ran on real data. Equal vs cap weight (17 pairs), the VIX curve, credit stress, dollar and 10-year yield with Alan's thesis, seasonality, and the Fed — including what prediction markets price for 28 Oct. Every average carries a 90% range; "not different" means the range includes the ordinary-day average. Green = up / better, red = down / worse. Nothing here says buy or sell.

On a phone, swipe a chart sideways to see all of it.

What the measurements say

  1. Equal weight is at or near its weakest ever against cap weight in 7 of the live pairs (RSP/SPY, QQEW/QQQ, QQQE/QQQ, EQAL/IWB, RSPS/XLP, RSPD/XLY, RSPC/XLC) — the ratio sits in the bottom 5% of its own history. RSP/SPY is at the <1st percentile of 23 years. What followed past stretches this far below the ratio's own 200-day average was mixed: for RSP/SPY the ratio a year later was up in 42.9% of 7 cases (median -0.2%). A low reading has not, by itself, meant equal weight catches up.
  2. The VIX curve is calm, not inverted. VIX 14.87 ÷ 3-month VIX 17.93 = 0.829 (inverted means above 1.0). It was inverted on 10.9% of days since 2006, last on 7 Apr 2026. An inversion comes with a sharp fall; it does not flag the low in advance. 43 of 60 S&P swing lows of 5% or more came during or just after an inversion, but any session of a comparable fall (SPY 5%+ below its 21-day high) sits in those same windows 77.2% of the time — the lows are no more likely to be there than any other day of the fall — and none came before the inversion began (35 during, 8 after). SPY's returns after inverted days were higher on average but the range is too wide to call it different.
  3. Credit is not stressed. Junk bonds vs investment grade (HYG ÷ LQD, with interest) is 0.1% off its all-time high. In the 41 S&P drops of 7% or more since 2007, this ratio peaked before the S&P top in 23 (median 22 sessions earlier) — by chance the same measurement shows it "first" 45.8% of the time.
  4. Alan's thesis, measured (not assumed) — no clear answer at one year. S&P days 5–10% below their 1-year high while the 10-year yield sat in the top third of its own last decade: a year later the S&P averaged +5.1% since 1971 against +11.6% with low yields, and +14.8% against +11.1% since 1990 — but a one-year result from overlapping days rests on only 18 (1971→) and 6 (1990→) separate years, and every one of those ranges overlaps the ordinary-day average. Over the next 63 sessions since 1990, high-yield pullbacks were followed by +5.5% (better than usual) — but so were low-yield ones (+4.3%, better than usual): any 5–10% pullback was, so high yields did not set them apart. "Overbought is overbought regardless of the story": since 1971, overbought days (RSI ≥ 70) with yields rising were followed by -0.4% over 63 sessions (worse than usual) vs +3.6% with yields falling — the story did matter there; since 1990 the two (+1.5% vs +2.5%) are not clearly different, which fits the thesis.
  5. Today's backdrop: 10-year yield 5.18%, above its 200-day average (4.42%) and at the 100th percentile of the last 10 years; dollar 101.04, above its 200-day. Since 1971, "yield up + dollar up" was the weakest of the four combinations for the S&P over the next 63 sessions (+0.9% vs +2.3% for all days).
  6. September is the one month with a real negative record (1928→: average -1.1%, up 44.9% of years; 90% range of the average -2.10 to -0.24); over the last 30 years its range includes zero. Option-expiry weeks and pre-holiday sessions have small positive averages; the week after expiry is flat.
  7. The Fed: both prediction markets price a 25 bp hike on 28 Oct — Kalshi 67.0%, Polymarket 65.5% (hold: 33.0% / 33.5%). Since 1994 the S&P rose on decision days more than on ordinary days (+0.23% vs +0.04%); in the 2013→ hikes the day after the decision averaged -0.60% (21 hikes).

Pivot lows: of the 60 SPY swing lows that ended a fall of 5% or more (pivots on closes, 10 sessions each side), 43 (71.7%) came during an inversion or within two weeks of one ending. That looks strong against the 33.0% of all sessions those windows cover, but that is the wrong comparison: a swing low is by definition a day deep in a fall, and a sharp fall is what inverts the curve. The fair comparison is other days of a comparable fall:

Sessions since 2006 where SPY closed …sessionsshare inside an inversion window
any session—33.0%
5% or more below its 21-session closing high67577.2%
5% or more below its 63-session closing high1,16972.3%
7% or more below its 21-session closing high37785.1%
the 60 swing lows6071.7%

The swing lows sit in those windows no more often than any other day of a comparable fall. Timing of the 43: 0 came before the inversion began, 35 during it, 8 in the two weeks after it ended. So the inversion arrives with the fall and has not given advance notice of the low. 58 of 77 inversion episodes had such a low (any depth) nearby.

Thesis 1 · "High yields + a pullback = a stronger buy zone"

"High" = the 10-year yield in the top third of its own previous 10 years (it is at the 100th percentile today); "low" = bottom third. "Pullback" = the S&P's close that far below its highest close of the past year. Checked twice: the full record since 1971, and since 1990 (the 1970s had high yields and a poor market for their own reasons).

Decision day move: the median absolute S&P move was 0.63% on decision days vs 0.53% on all days. Dates: the Fed's own published schedules (scheduled meetings only; the emergency moves of 3 and 15 Mar 2020 are left out); hike / hold / cut from FMP's decision rows, which start in 2013. Recent: 29 Oct 2025 -0.25 · 10 Dec 2025 -0.25 · 28 Jan 2026 0 · 18 Mar 2026 0 · 29 Apr 2026 0 · 17 Jun 2026 0 · 29 Jul 2026 0 · 16 Sep 2026 +0.25. Next: 28 Oct 2026 · 9 Dec 2026 · 27 Jan 2027.

What could be wrong

  • Overlap. Forward returns from neighbouring days share most of their future, so thousands of "days" are really a few dozen episodes. The ranges resample whole blocks of the calendar at least as long as the window being measured — months for 5–21 sessions, quarters for 63, half-years for 126, years for 252 — and the tables show how many separate blocks sit behind each number. With fewer than 5 the page says "too few to judge"; treat anything under ~10 as a hint. The one-year rows therefore carry wide ranges: a year-long result from 1990 onward has only about 36 separate years to draw on in total.
  • Thresholds are choices. "High yields" (top third of 10 years), "pullback" (5–10% below the 1-year high), RSI 70, 10% above the 200-day, the 5% extremes of each ratio — each is one reasonable cut, stated on the page, not a discovered number. The 4%-yield rows are there to show how much the answer moves with the cut.
  • Different eras. 1971–1989 had inflation and rising rates; the 1990 → rows exist because the answer changes with the era.
  • Price only. No dividends in the S&P, SPY or equal-vs-cap ratios; the credit ratios do include interest (they would drift otherwise).
  • Pivots on closes. The chart API's SPY history carries some impossible wick prints (e.g. 2 Jun 2009 low 87.53 against a close of 94.87), so swing points here use closing prices, not wicks.
  • Prediction markets are thin next to futures and move with news; the odds are a snapshot at 2026-09-28T13:18:14Z.
  • HYG on the chart API before 2007-04-11. The chart API serves HYG from 2004-02-04 at about $25.1; the iShares high-yield fund only launched on 2007-04-11 (at about $104). The early stretch is a different instrument under a reused ticker. This study uses FMP's dividend-adjusted HYG, which starts 2007-04-11.
  • QQQ on the chart API has a hole 2004-11-30 → 2011-03-23. The Nasdaq-100 fund traded as QQQQ in those years; the chart API's QQQ series skips them. The Nasdaq pairs here use FMP for both legs.
  • Equal-weight sector funds (RSPT, RSPF, RSPC …) on the chart API start 2023-06-07. Invesco renamed them in 2023 (RYT→RSPT etc.). FMP carries the full history under the new tickers, split-adjusted; on the 829 overlapping sessions FMP and the chart API agree to within 0.02%.
  • Mid- and small-cap equal-weight funds stopped. FMP's last prints: EWMC 2023-10-05, EWSC 2023-04-06 (zero volume). No live US mid/small equal-weight vs cap-weight pair was found on FMP; those two rows are history only.
  • XLF's 2016 spin-off. On 2016-09-19 XLF handed its real-estate holdings to its owners as the new XLRE fund. The chart API's XLF drops about 7% that day with no loss to holders. This study scales XLF's bars before that day by 0.931 (its move that day relative to SPY), so the RSPF ÷ XLF line has no false step.
  • Thin trading in 2008–2009 in the old equal-weight sector funds. Their closing prints then sometimes lagged the market by a day (e.g. RSPF ÷ XLF −15% then +26% on 28–29 Oct 2008). The jumps reverse the next day; they add noise to the 2008 ends of those lines and to the 'far below / far above' dots from that year.

What was not done

  • No Trendoscope diagonals or cloud-order combinations with the VIX curve yet — only pivots and RSI. The inversion/low coincidence measured in section 2 does not by itself justify that work: the lows are no more common in inversion windows than any other day of a comparable fall.
  • No international equal-vs-cap pair (none found on FMP with history); no live mid- or small-cap pair (both Invesco funds stopped trading in 2023).
  • No official CME FedWatch odds (blocked; its terms forbid scraping). No paid source was used.
  • Hike / hold / cut split only from 2013 (FMP's decision rows start there); 1994–2012 meetings are in the totals without a type.
  • Nothing is weighted by relevance or market cap; no Hub panel was built (see the proposal); nothing was deployed and no database was touched.
